prompt.context: Your client, Lonestar Oil, is a large petroleum refining company that owns service stations. Lonestar is looking to expand, and is looking to run a service station in one of the main ports in Seattle. The CEO has hired you to determine how to proceed. The port is operating 24 hours per day. The port area is slowly growing because of consolidation occurring along Northwest ports. There are three existing service stations in the vicinity. These stations are of equal size and capabilities. Two of these are owned by major corporations like Lonestar Oil, and the third is family owned. Lonestar requires a 5-year payback on initial investment. Disregard cost of capital.
prompt.question: How should Lonestar Oil proceed with expanding into this Seattle port — should it build a new service station or pursue another approach? Does the investment meet the 5-year payback requirement?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current demand at the port?
clarifying_info.a: There is no concrete information on full demand, but estimates place demand between 15,000 and 20,000 gallons of gasoline per day for the port. All three existing stations are currently operating at full capacity.

clarifying_info.q: What are the capabilities of a new station?
clarifying_info.a: A new station can sell 5,000 gallons per day. It costs $650,000 in initial costs and includes a minimart.

clarifying_info.q: What is the gas price and margin?
clarifying_info.a: Gas sells for $3.00 per gallon. The station makes a margin of 10 cents per gallon.
It costs $250 per day to run the station (utilities, labor, etc.). Operating the minimart costs an additional $100 per day.
Daily minimart sales are $500. Daily cost of merchandise is $200.

clarifying_info.q: How many days per year should we assume?
Is there any option besides building a new station?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The family-owned station is for sale at $530,000, but it has no minimart. Building a minimart on that existing station would cost an additional $130,000. The other two corporate-owned stations are not for sale.

framework: Market analysis: assess current demand, capacity, and growth in the port area
Entry options: evaluate build-new vs. acquire-existing station
Revenue model: gas margin + minimart contribution
Cost structure: initial investment (capex) vs. ongoing fixed and variable operating costs
Payback analysis: 5-year cumulative profit vs. initial investment for each option
Qualitative factors: timing, competition, demand risk, expansion potential

questions.prompt: How much would a new gas station earn per year from gasoline sales alone?
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply margin per gallon by daily volume, subtract daily fixed costs, then annualize.

math.setup: Daily gas profit = (margin per gallon × gallons/day) − daily operating costs; Annual profit = daily profit × 300 days

questions.prompt: Including the minimart, what is the total annual profit for the new station, and does it meet the 5-year payback requirement?
questions.guidance: Candidate adds minimart daily profit (sales minus COGS minus operating cost) to gas profit, annualizes, and checks against the $650,000 initial investment over 5 years.

math.setup: Minimart daily profit = daily sales − daily merchandise cost − daily minimart operating cost; Total annual profit = (gas daily profit + minimart daily profit) × 300; 5-year profit vs. $650,000 capex
math.answer: $135,000/year; 5-year total = $675,000, which exceeds the $650,000 investment by $25,000 — payback requirement met

questions.prompt: If Lonestar buys the existing family-owned station (with and without adding a minimart), does the investment meet the 5-year payback requirement?
questions.guidance: Candidate should evaluate both sub-cases: (1) no minimart — $530,000 investment against gas-only profits; (2) with minimart — $660,000 total investment against full profits. Then compare to the build-new option.

math.setup: Option A (no minimart): $530,000 investment, gas-only profit $75,000/year × 5; Option B (with minimart): ($530,000 + $130,000) = $660,000 investment, full profit $135,000/year × 5
steps: Option A 5-year profit = $75,000 × 5 = $375,000 < $530,000 — does NOT meet payback
Compare: Build-new surplus = $25,000; Buy-and-add-minimart surplus = $15,000 → Build-new wins on financials alone
math.answer: Buying without minimart fails payback. Buying + adding minimart barely passes ($15,000 surplus) but is worse than building new ($25,000 surplus) on pure financials.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the pure payback numbers, what qualitative factors should Lonestar consider when deciding whether to build a new station or buy the existing one?

categories.name: Demand risk
ideas: Current demand (15,000–20,000 gal/day) may not support a fourth station; buying is safer since it captures existing share rather than adding supply
Demand is growing due to port consolidation, which could favor building in the long run

categories.name: Timing
ideas: Building a new station takes longer than acquiring an existing one; buying enables faster revenue generation
Permitting and construction delays add uncertainty to the build option

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: A competitor could buy the family-owned station if Lonestar delays; acquiring now blocks that entry
Adding a fourth station (build) may erode margins across all four stations if demand is insufficient
Buying deters new entrants since it does not add net capacity

categories.name: Expansion potential
ideas: The existing station could have more pumps added to satisfy demand growth
New station could also be sized for expansion from the outset

categories.name: Marketing and differentiation
ideas: Adding a minimart drives incremental traffic and differentiates Lonestar from the three competitors that lack one
Minimart variety and quality can shift market share beyond the new station's natural demand

categories.name: Next steps
ideas: Conduct closer demand analysis to confirm whether the port can support a fourth station before committing to build
Negotiate purchase price of family-owned station; $530,000 asking price may have room

recommendation: On pure financials, building a new station with a minimart is the better option ($25,000 surplus over 5 years vs. $15,000 for buy-and-add-minimart)
However, qualitative factors — faster time-to-revenue, competitive blocking, and lower demand risk — favor acquiring the existing family-owned station and adding a minimart

Recommended path: acquire the existing station for $530,000 and invest $130,000 to add a minimart ($660,000 total), then prioritize demand analysis to evaluate whether future capacity expansion is warranted
risks: Demand may not grow enough to support all four stations, potentially compressing margins
Build-new option risks a competitor acquiring the family-owned station in the interim
Buying may delay ability to expand if the acquired footprint is limited
next_steps: Commission a detailed demand study to quantify port traffic growth and assess whether four stations are sustainable
Negotiate the purchase price of the family-owned station below $530,000 to improve the payback margin
Develop a minimart format and SKU strategy tailored to the port's customer mix (truck drivers, maritime workers)
Evaluate pump-expansion options on the acquired site to capture growing demand without building from scratch
